{{Short description|Point in a topological space}}
In [[topology]], a '''dispersion point'''{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1978|p=33}}{{sfn|Abry|Dijkstra|van Mill|2007|p=726}} of a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> is a point <math>p\in X</math> such that <math>X</math> is [[connected (topology)|connected]] and removing the point leaves <math>X\setminus\{p\}</math> [[totally disconnected]] (meaning that its [[connected component (topology)|connected component]]s are all singletons, i.e., <math>X\setminus\{p\}</math> contains no connected subset of size at least two).

Examples of spaces with a dispersion point include:
* the [[Knaster–Kuratowski fan]],{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1978|loc=counterexample 128, items 1 and 2}}
* spaces with a [[particular point topology]],
* spaces with an [[excluded point topology]].

A connected space <math>X</math> with <math>|X|\ge 3</math> can have at most one dispersion point.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kline |first1=John |title=A theorem concerning connected point sets |journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae |date=1922 |volume=3 |pages=238–239 |doi=10.4064/fm-3-1-238-239}}</ref>
The case <math>|X|=2</math> (covering [[Sierpiński space]] and an [[indiscrete space]] of size two) is a degenerate case, where every point of <math>X</math> is a dispersion point (because removing a point leaves a singleton, which is totally disconnected).

== Explosion point ==

An '''explosion point'''{{sfn|Abry|Dijkstra|van Mill|2007|p=726}} of a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> is a point <math>p\in X</math> such that <math>X</math> is [[connected (topology)|connected]] and removing the point leaves <math>X\setminus\{p\}</math> [[totally separated]] (meaning that for any two distinct points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> there is a [[clopen set]] containing <math>x</math> and not <math>y</math>).

Every explosion point is a dispersion point (because totally separated spaces are totally disconnected).

Examples of spaces with an explosion point include spaces with a [[particular point topology]] and spaces with an [[excluded point topology]].
The [[Knaster–Kuratowski fan]] has a dispersion point which is not an explosion point.{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1978|loc=counterexample 129, item 3}}

A space of size at least three can have at most one explosion point.

If ''p'' is an explosion point for a space ''X'', then the totally separated space <math>X\setminus \{p\}</math> is said to be ''pulverized''.
